title: Dying to Self
subtitle: What it costs to decide "your will be done" when the heart is still afraid

key_verse.text: Then said Jesus unto his disciples, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.

cards.title: The One Who Walked Away Sad
cards.subtitle: He understood everything. And still could not decide.
cards.content:
There is a man in the Gospels who did everything right and walked away sad.

He listened to Jesus in silence. He accepted every word as true. He felt the full weight of what was being asked of him. He heard the invitation, understood it clearly, and walked away sad.

🔍 What makes this moment unique:
This man had kept the commandments since his youth. He truly sought God. He was sincere, someone who had done things right up to that moment.

And yet, facing the final decision, his body moved in a direction different from what his mind had understood.

This reveals something every person who has seriously tried to follow God recognizes: **understanding God's will and deciding to do it are two different acts.** A person can have all the theology clear, all the doctrine in place, and still stand frozen at the door without walking through it.

📍 The question that opens this study:
What makes deciding so different from understanding? Why can the heart be convinced and, at the same time, unable to move?

Matthew 19 answers this question step by step, showing real people facing this same crossroads: a child, a rich young man, a group of disciples who left everything. In each of them appears the same question you may be asking yourself today: what does it truly take to say, "your will be done," no matter what happens?

scripture_references.text: But when the young man heard that saying, he went away sorrowful: for he had great possessions.

cards.revelation_key: Understanding God's will is the first step. Deciding to do it, whatever it costs, is the step this study wants to help you take.

cards.title: The One Who Has Nothing to Negotiate
cards.subtitle: Before you can let go of something, you must recognize you never owned anything
cards.content:
Before speaking of the rich young man, Jesus sets before his disciples a scene that seems small, but holds the key to everything that follows.

People were bringing children to him so he might lay his hands on them and pray, and the disciples turned them away — probably thinking Jesus had more important matters to attend to. Jesus responds firmly in Matthew 19:14, commanding that they be allowed to come to him, for of such is the kingdom of heaven.

🔍 Why the child is the model:
In the first-century world, the child was the person with the least power, the least legal voice, and the least ability to negotiate their own place in society. They depended entirely on others for food, protection, and provision.

Jesus is not praising the moral innocence of the child — every human being is born with a nature that needs to be transformed. He is pointing to something different: the child **receives** because they have nothing to buy with, nothing to negotiate, nothing to secure on their own.

🔄 A logic opposite to ours:
In first-century society, as in ours, power and status opened doors. A child had neither — nothing to negotiate, nothing to offer in exchange for a place in the Kingdom.

And yet Jesus declares that the Kingdom belongs exactly to those in that position. He does not give it to those who have the most to offer, but to those who have the least. Measured by human logic, this decision defies every category of investment: the Kingdom is given as a pure gift to those who have nothing to pay with. God acts here out of love and grace — an undeserved gift — and the only thing we can truly give back is worship and wonder, not payment. A gift earned by merit would stop being a gift — it would become a transaction. The Kingdom is given to those who have nothing to buy it with: that is what makes it a pure gift.

👑 The connection to the decision to die to self:
This is the foundation on which everything else in the chapter is built. A person can let go of possessions, plans, or control only after first recognizing their total dependence on God. The posture of the child comes first because it prepares the ground for the decision that follows: that of a young man who does have much to negotiate, and who will discover how much it costs him to let it go.

scripture_references.text: But Jesus said, Allow little children, and forbid them not, to come unto me: for of such is the kingdom of heaven.

cards.revelation_key: The Kingdom is offered to those who have the least to negotiate with — that is the proof that it is grace, not a transaction.

cards.title: Loved and Called in the Same Instant
cards.subtitle: Jesus calls precisely where he loves most deeply
cards.content:
The young man who approaches Jesus brings an honest question in Matthew 19:16: what good thing he must do to have eternal life. After keeping the commandments his whole life, he still feels something is missing.

That final question — *what do I still lack?* — is the question of a sincere man who genuinely wants to know what he is missing.

📖 The detail only Mark records:
The parallel account in Mark adds a key detail: in Mark 10:21, Jesus looks at him and loves him before saying another word. What follows is born from that love: the invitation to sell what he has, give it to the poor, and follow him, with the promise of treasure in heaven.

🕊️ A call that leaves him free:
Jesus looks at him, loves him, and says: "one thing you lack" — that love is precisely what leads him to ask this of him, because he sees something in his riches that competes for the place only God occupies in a heart. The young man chooses to walk away sad, and Jesus does not stop him: the freedom to decide is part of love, because without it there would be no decision to love, only automatic obedience. The young man sees clearly what he has today. What he cannot yet see is the treasure in heaven that Jesus promises him in exchange — because the temporal can be touched, and the eternal can still only be believed.

scripture_references.text: And, behold, one came and said unto him, Good Teacher, what good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life? And he said unto him, Why do you call me good? there is none good but one, that is, God: but if you will enter into life, keep the commandments. He said unto him, Which? Jesus said, You shall do no murder, You shall not commit adultery, You shall not steal, You shall not bear false witness, Honor your father and your mother: and, You shall love your neighbor as yourself. The young man said unto him, All these things have I kept from my youth up: what lack I yet?

Then Jesus beholding him loved him, and said unto him, One thing you lack: go your way, sell whatsoever you have, and give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven: and come, take up the cross, and follow me.

cards.revelation_key: The love of Jesus does not stop before what costs you most to let go — and it leaves you truly free to decide what you will do with that call.

cards.title: What He Had and What He Felt
cards.subtitle: The Greek reveals why letting go hurts like losing an identity
cards.content:
The final verse of the encounter, in Matthew 19:22, narrates that the young man went away sad because he had great possessions. Two words from the original Greek show precisely what was at stake.

💎 **κτήματα** (ktémata)
Transliteration: *ktémata*
Meaning: describes **real estate, properties, and lands** — the kind of possession that gave status, inheritance, and lasting social security in his culture.
Revelation: what Jesus asked him to let go of was the entire foundation of his identity and his place in the world.

😔 **λυπούμενος** (lypoumenos)
Transliteration: *lypoumenos*
Meaning: **grieved, deeply pained** — a genuine sorrow that settles in the chest.
Revelation: his sadness confirms he had understood Jesus's offer perfectly. He went away grieving, because he understood exactly what was being asked and what it would mean to give it up.

📍 The connection to today's decision:
These two words together reveal something important: the decision to let go of control hurts precisely because what is at stake is understood clearly. The rich young man knew exactly what was in the balance — but he could only see one side of it.

His possessions were stable, known, present. The eternal treasure Jesus offered him in exchange required faith, just as Hebrews 11:6 confirms. Letting go of the temporal for the eternal is an act of faith. And what is offered in exchange is the greatest of all rewards: eternity with God.

greek_words.meaning: real estate, properties, possessions that gave status and social security
greek_words.revelation: What Jesus asked him to let go of was the entire foundation of his identity.
His pain confirms he understood exactly what Jesus's invitation would cost.

scripture_references.text: But when the young man heard that saying, he went away sorrowful: for he had great possessions.
But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that comes to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him.

cards.revelation_key: The pain of letting go is proof that you understood exactly what you were giving up — and letting go of it by faith is what opens the way to the greatest of all rewards.

cards.title: A Decision of the Will
cards.subtitle: Taking up the cross is decided even while fear is still present
cards.content:
Jesus describes the call with a concrete image in Matthew 16:24: whoever wants to follow him must deny himself, take up his cross, and follow him. In the first century, no one heard the word "cross" as a soft metaphor — it was the instrument of a public execution. Jesus chose that image on purpose: it describes the total end of the right to rule one's own life.

⚖️ A surrender weighed with the heart:
It is easy to pray "your will be done" without ever having truly thought it through. But God's will can ask for concrete and costly things: years of work, a house, a secure income, what has been built with effort. Hebrews 11:1 defines faith (πίστις, *pistis*) as the assurance of things hoped for and the conviction of things not seen — and that assurance does not remove fear, it moves through it.

The rich young man understood the invitation with complete clarity and still could not walk through the door. The disciples did: they left family, wives, children, the trade that sustained them — and thanks to that surrender, generation after generation, there are people serving God today who would not exist without that heavy, sustained "yes" given centuries ago.

📖 The promise that sustains the decision:
To those who do decide to let go, Jesus promises in Matthew 19:29 that they will receive a hundredfold and inherit eternal life. And he goes further, speaking of the **palingenesia** (παλιγγενεσία) — the complete restoration of all things, the moment when today's sacrifice is revealed as an eternal investment.

✝️ Jesus himself lived it first:
In Gethsemane, Jesus felt the real weight of what was coming and prayed: "O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as you will" (Matthew 26:39). The spirit was willing, but the flesh was weak (Matthew 26:41) — the same tension felt by anyone today facing a difficult decision. Jesus did not pretend to have no fear. He felt it, said it in prayer, and still surrendered his will. Because of that decision, there is now access to the Father and eternal life through him.

🙏 The decision left in your hands today:
Doing God's will no matter what happens is a decision made with fear still present — as Jesus himself made it in the garden — trusting that the One who invites you to surrender is the same One who already showed, looking at and loving the rich young man, that his call is born from a love that seeks to give you more than what it asks you to let go of.

scripture_references.text: Then said Jesus unto his disciples, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.
Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen.

And everyone that has forsaken houses, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my name's sake, shall receive a hundredfold, and shall inherit everlasting life.
And he went a little farther, and fell on his face, and prayed, saying, O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as you will.
Watch and pray, that you enter not into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.

cards.revelation_key: The decision to do God's will is made with fear still present — as Jesus himself made it in Gethsemane — because faith is taking the step, not waiting for the trembling to go away.

discovery_questions.question: What possession, plan, or security occupies today the place that property occupied in the rich young man's life?
In what area of your life do you find it hardest to adopt the posture of the child — receiving instead of negotiating your own place with God?
If faith means taking the step while fear is still present, what concrete decision do you need to make today, even though the trembling has not gone away?
When you say "your will be done, Lord," do you say it from the heart, knowing God is real and can ask something concrete of you — or do you say it as a phrase you haven't yet weighed?

prayer.title: Prayer to Decide with Fear Still Present
prayer.content:
Father, I come to you recognizing that many times I understand your will clearly and still find it hard to decide to do it. Like the young man who walked away sad, sometimes I would rather hold on to what is known than let it go into your hands.

Thank you that your gaze toward me is the same one you had toward him: a gaze that loves first and asks afterward, always seeking my freedom and not my limitation. Give me today a heart like a child's, one that knows how to receive from you instead of negotiating with you.

When fear appears before the decision to do your will, give me the faith to take the step with the trembling still present, trusting that your love sustains everything I give you.

Today I want to say "your will be done" from the heart, as a real and considered decision. If you ask me to let go of what today holds my security — my job, my house, what I have built — I want to be able to say yes, because I trust that what you have prepared is worth more than all of that together. Maybe you will never ask me to let go of everything, but you see my heart, and today I want you to find a true surrender there. You promised that whoever leaves something for you receives much more in return, and that "much more" — having you, having eternal life — is the greatest prize there is.

In the name of Jesus, who took up the cross and showed me the way,

Amen.
